extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent applicants, and law students practicing or studying U.S. patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and substantive requirements governing what subject-matter may be included in a U.S. patent application (oath, disclosure, enablement, novelty/double-patenting, joinder, divisional practice, abandonment/dedication, reissue remedy). Focused on U.S. practice and judicial interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of foreign patents
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant must disclose all his foreign patents for the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure must be definite and in the usual form. The rule requiring disclosure of the date of foreign patents is reasonable and authorized by statute; examples and citations: Ex parte Mason (1888), Ex parte Toufflin (1879). The affidavit concerning foreign patents is only presumptive evidence of inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application oath as prima facie evidence of inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The application-oath is prima facie evidence that the applicant is the first and original inventor and in uncontested Patent Office proceedings is conclusive as to matters to which it relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where rival applications with contradictory oaths are filed, the affidavits neutralize each other and the question remains open to further proof. Averments about foreign patents add nothing additional to the force of the oath as evidence of originality. Case citations: Parker v. Stiles; Ex parte Nagel (1880).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of the application oath
rubrics_metrics.description: An application-oath relates only to the inventions for which a patent is solicited; it concerns the whole application (e.g., joint application relates to the whole), not separate parts of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An oath that another had obtained a patent (e.g., in England) is conclusive evidence that the applicant is sole inventor until contrary appears. The oath does not relate to a model. See Ex parte Cran-dall (1886), Tieman, Simpson & Collins (1877).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of false oath or omission
rubrics_metrics.description: A false oath of citizenship is an irremediable defect that avoids the patent; but omission of the oath does not necessarily invalidate a granted patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a patent issues the Patent Office generally lacks jurisdiction to inquire whether the application-oath was true or false. A recital in the patent that the oath was taken is conclusive until fraud is shown. Case citations: Child v. Adams (1854); Ex parte Oillen (1877); Crompton v. Belknap Mills (1869).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter must be a patentable invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must claim a patentable invention: a concrete art, instrument, or process within the statutory classes that is new, useful, and not abandoned to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing less than a statutory patentable invention can be the subject of an application. The application must describe the invention and the manner and process of making/using it in full, clear, concise, and exact terms to enable a person skilled in the art to construct and use it. Drawings or a model must be provided when required by the Commissioner. See Ex parte Stair v. Farmer (1888).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must file a written description, with drawings/models if required, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description must show the invention is complete and capable of useful operation; actual reduction to practice is not necessary if the application shows adequate disclosure and that inventor has prosecuted the application diligently and believed in its importance. Impracticable inventions must be rejected. See Stair v. Farmer; Ex parte De Bausset (1888).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention must be capable of useful operation
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be perfected and capable of useful operation to be patentable; impracticable or incapable inventions must be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner must be able to find the invention useful and important; mere speculative or non-operative concepts are not patentable. Cases: Ex parte De Bausset; Stair v. Farmer.

rubrics_metrics.name: No two patents to same inventor for the same invention (double patenting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two U.S. patents cannot be granted to the same inventor for the same invention; if issued the later is absolutely void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The government's power to create a monopoly is exhausted by the first grant. The date of applications is immaterial; the later patent is void where scope is the same. See McMillin v. Rees and multiple Ex parte authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior U.S. patent to rival or foreign patent by same inventor (when not a bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent issued to a rival inventor is not necessarily a bar to a later patent to the true inventor; a prior foreign patent does not always prevent issuance of a broader American patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the earlier U.S. patent was granted to one who was not the true original inventor, that patent does not bar the true inventor's later patent. A prior foreign patent may limit term or practice but does not automatically invalidate a U.S. patent or bar a broader claim. See Hibbard v. Richmond; Faore v. Bradley; Kendrick v. Emmons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter must not include matter already patented by the same inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: An application that includes matter already patented in the U.S. by the same inventor (even together with new matter) is within the rule against double patenting; the application must distinguish the earlier invention and claim only the new invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor who improves his own patented invention cannot obtain a patent for the entire improved invention covering previously patented elements — he may only claim the new development. It may be necessary to describe the earlier patent fully but the new application must clearly show it seeks patent only for the last invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: New use of previously patented invention (same inventor)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application by the same inventor asserting patents for newly discovered uses of his previously patented invention is generally forbidden unless the new use itself involves inventive skill and qualifies as a new patentable art or combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All uses that can be put to an invention without additional inventive skill are covered by the original patent. If a new use is discovered by inventive effort, that new use may be patentable as a new art or combination, but the application must distinguish the old invention from the new one and claim only the latter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue remedy for defective prior patent (not new independent patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior patent is defective, inoperative, or ambiguous, the proper remedy is reissue of that patent rather than a new patent for the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application for a new patent covering matter that can be cured by re-issue of the former patent is improper; reissue is the adequate remedy. See discussion: reissue vs. new patent doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral parts/combinations and option to separate patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a concrete invention is composed of parts each resulting from separate inventive acts, the inventor may choose to obtain separate patents for each part or one patent for the whole; but if the first patent clearly confers monopoly as to all, later patents for parts may be barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventor's first application/patent attempted to claim all subordinate inventions and the government conferred an all-encompassing monopoly, no later application for those parts can be entertained; otherwise, separate patents may be possible. Distinguish unitary inventions (must be protected as whole) from composite inventions (parts separable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation, divisional practice, and concurrent applications to avoid abandonment inference
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant who desires to preserve rights to distinct, independent features described but not claimed in a first application should expressly reserve the right to file another application (divisional) and prosecute it without delay, or have concurrent pendency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to claim subject-matter shown and described may lead to an inference of abandonment or dedication to the public unless reservation and reasonable diligence in filing a later/divisional application occurs. Filing a second application during pendency anticipates and prevents the inference of dedication. See Ex parte Roberts and related practice guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment/dedication to the public (effect of description without claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter described but not claimed in a patent may be treated as abandoned or dedicated to the public if accompanied by public use/sale for two years or other circumstances indicating dedication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere description in a prior patent does not inevitably preclude later patenting of that described but unclaimed matter; loss of right typically requires evidence of abandonment or dedication (e.g., two years' public use/sale), but courts infer intent to dedicate in some classes of divisional cases. Practice prefers permitting later patents unless dedication/abandonment is shown. Cases and tensions discussed: James v. Campbell, Vulcanite Paving Co. v. American Artificial Stone Paving Co., Vermont Farm Machine Co. v. Marble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must prosecute new/divisional applications with reasonable diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid the conclusive inference that described-but-unclaimed subject-matter was dedicated, an applicant should file subsequent applications (divisional or separate) promptly; reasonable time and diligence are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may file a reservation and prosecute a second application so it is pending concurrently with the first; such course prevents the inference of dedication. Courts have sustained the practice of permitting later applications where reservation and reasonable diligence are shown. See Ex parte Atwood; practice notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder rules — limiting application by prior claims and preventing improper aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: The law and office practice include rules that compel an applicant to limit his application by the claims of patents he has previously obtained and rules that govern the joinder of separate inventions in a single application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants cannot extend the life of a patent by reserving unclaimed portions and later claiming them; joinder rules and divisionals control proper aggregation. If features are independent, divisional applications or reservations should be used to separate claims; the Office has required applicants to file separate applications for matter shown but not properly patentable in the original application.
